claim: The 1st Marine Division under Major General Alexander Vandegrift landed on Guadalcanal and Tulagi on 7 August 1942; the airfield was taken and renamed Henderson Field
source: Wikipedia and HistoryNet summaries of the Guadalcanal campaign
note: Only the dates and the commander were read; unit lists are from memory.

claim: Fletcher withdrew the three carriers on the evening of 8 August, citing fuel and the exposure of his carriers; Turner took the transports out on 9 August with part of the cargo still aboard
source: HistoryNet, 'Why the United States lost Guadalcanal'; National WWII Museum, 'War on a Shoestring'
note: Sources differ on whether the cargo left aboard was a quarter or more; the screen says 'a part'.

claim: About twenty aircraft were lost in the first two days (the United States lost 19 over the two days, in combat and accidents)
source: pacificeagles.net, The Guadalcanal Landings; NHHC H-Gram 010 on Fletcher's fighter losses
note: The common figure of 21 of 99 Wildcats was not found in a source read today; the report says 'about twenty aircraft'.

claim: Coastwatchers on Bougainville and New Georgia reported the Rabaul bombers on both days; Lieutenant Commander Eric Feldt directed the Coastwatching Service
source: Solomon Islands Encyclopaedia; Navy Victoria Network (Paul Mason's warning on 7 August: 'twenty-four bombers headed yours'); Wikipedia, Eric Feldt
note: Feldt directed the Coastwatching Service from Townsville.

claim: The Guadalcanal Japanese were mostly construction troops and withdrew west; the Tulagi, Gavutu and Tanambogo garrisons fought to the last
source: From memory of the standard histories
note: Still unchecked: not searched in this round.

claim: Report times 0613 and 0910 (naval fire and first landing)
source: From memory
note: The report times are modeled dispatch times, not quotations.

claim: The submarines Darter and Dace sank the heavy cruisers Atago and Maya on 23 October 1944; Musashi was sunk by carrier aircraft on 24 October after about 19 torpedo and 17 bomb hits
source: USNI Naval History, 'Leyte Gulf: Pacific War's greatest battle'; Britannica

claim: Nishimura's Southern Force, with the battleships Fuso and Yamashiro, was destroyed in Surigao Strait on the night of 24 to 25 October and Nishimura was killed; Shima turned back
source: Britannica; Naval History and Heritage Command

claim: Ozawa's carriers drew Halsey north on 24 to 25 October; four Japanese carriers were sunk off Cape Engano on 25 October
source: Britannica; Naval History and Heritage Command

claim: Kurita's flagship was Yamato after Atago was lost; Kurita turned back briefly on 24 October and went through San Bernardino Strait in the night
source: Wikipedia summary of the battle

claim: Onishi commanded the First Air Fleet on Luzon from October 1944; the Second Air Fleet under Fukudome on Formosa lost most of its strength in the Formosa air battle of 12 to 16 October 1944
source: Wikipedia, Takijiro Onishi and Formosa Air Battle; USNI Proceedings, 'Strategic aspects of the Battle of Formosa'
note: The report no longer says the Second Air Fleet flew in to the Philippines.

claim: About 21,000 defenders under Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi; tunnels of about eleven miles; each man ordered to kill ten of the enemy
source: Warfare History Network; WorldWar2Database

claim: Rear Admiral Toshinosuke Ichimaru commanded the Navy troops on Iwo Jima; Colonel Baron Takeichi Nishi commanded the 26th Tank Regiment, whose tanks were first dug in and then used in local counterattacks; Nishi was killed in March
source: HyperWar, Japanese order of battle at Iwo Jima; Wikipedia, Takeichi Nishi; Osprey, 'Tanks on Iwo Jima 1945'
note: One source gives the admiral's first name as Rinosuke; the written form is the same and the reading is unresolved. The report no longer gives a tank count.

claim: The Marines announced the capture of Iwo Jima on 14 March; the last Japanese attack came on the night of 25 to 26 March (about 250 Japanese were found dead near the lines on 26 March); the island was declared secured on 26 March
source: History.com, 'Fighting on Iwo Jima ends'; USMC Iwo Jima monograph
note: About 200 prisoners comes from the earlier Iwo Jima report and was not rechecked. The earlier date of 16 March was removed.

claim: The 28th Marines took the summit of Mount Suribachi on 23 February
source: History.com; USMC Iwo Jima monograph (28th Marines; raising of the flag about 10:00 on 23 February)
note: The hour differs between sources; the report gives none.

claim: The Marines asked for ten days of naval bombardment and were given three; fewer than 200 of about 915 estimated fortifications had been silenced when the Marines landed
source: Warfare History Network summary of the battle
note: The 915 and 200 figures are from one account.

claim: The V Amphibious Corps under Major General Harry Schmidt landed the 4th and 5th Marine Divisions on 19 February with the 3rd Marine Division in reserve; Rear Admiral William Blandy commanded the Amphibious Support Force; Vice Admiral Richmond Kelly Turner commanded the Joint Expeditionary Force
source: Wikipedia, Harry Schmidt; NPS/USMC Marines in WWII series; HyperWar, US order of battle at Iwo Jima; Wikipedia, USS Bismarck Sea
note: Turner was Vice Admiral and led Task Force 51; Blandy led Task Force 52. The 3rd Marine Division was the corps reserve and its 21st Marines landed on 21 February. Bismarck Sea was sunk by two kamikaze hits on 21 February.

claim: Operation Ten-Go: Yamato, the cruiser Yahagi and eight destroyers under Vice Admiral Seiichi Ito sailed on 6 April 1945; carrier aircraft sank Yamato on 7 April; about 3,055 of her crew were lost
source: Wikipedia, Operation Ten-Go and Seiichi Ito; warhistory.org
note: The death toll varies from about 2,500 to 3,060 between sources. The screen says about 3,000.

claim: Kikusui No. 1 (6 and 7 April) used about 355 kamikaze aircraft; ten Kikusui attacks were flown between April and June
source: Wikipedia, Operation Kikusui

claim: Lieutenant General Mitsuru Ushijima's Thirty-Second Army defended in depth around Shuri and made a counteroffensive on 4 and 5 May that failed; Vice Admiral Matome Ugaki commanded the Fifth Air Fleet; Admiral Soemu Toyoda commanded the Combined Fleet
source: HyperWar, US Army Okinawa volume ch. XII (the 4 May counteroffensive); Wikipedia, Operation Kikusui; Wikipedia, Matome Ugaki
note: That Toyoda commanded the Combined Fleet was not searched today.

claim: Of 101 destroyers and similar ships on the radar picket stations, 10 were sunk and 32 damaged by kamikaze attacks; just over 4,900 Navy personnel were killed in the campaign
source: Rielly, Kamikazes, Corsairs and Picket Ships (via the author's summary page); Naval History and Heritage Command H-Grams on Okinawa
note: The scopes of the sources differ (picket duty only against the whole campaign).

claim: Landing craft armed with guns and rockets were sent to the picket stations from April; Major General Francis Mulcahy commanded the Tactical Air Force of the Tenth Army; Vice Admiral Marc Mitscher commanded Task Force 58; repair ships worked at Kerama Retto
source: Rielly, Kamikazes, Corsairs and Picket Ships (15 stations; LCS(L) support from 2 April); Wikipedia, Tactical Air Force Tenth Army (Mulcahy, later relieved by Woods); NHHC H-Grams; Kerama Retto as 'Busted Ship Bay'
note: The repair commander at Okinawa is now Vice Admiral William W. Smith, who took the Service Force on 6 March 1945. That Mitscher led Task Force 58 was not searched.
